Climate change makes November heat five times more likely in parts of South Africa
Human-caused climate change has significantly increased the likelihood of unusually high temperatures forecast across parts of South Africa between 10 and 13 November, according to a Climate Central analysis
Climate change has made the unusually intense November heat forecast across parts of South Africa this week at least five times more likely in some areas, according to an analysis by climate science organisation Climate Central.
The analysis, using its Climate Shift Index, found that climate change had significantly increased the likelihood of extreme heat forecast across the country between 10 and 13 November.
The index reached its highest level, five, in Upington, Bloemfontein and Rustenburg, indicating that climate change had made the extreme heat at least five times more likely in these cities.
About 26 million people across South Africa were expected to experience at least one day of extreme heat with a Climate Shift Index of three or higher during the four days, it said.
More than 660 000km², or about 54% of the country’s land area, was forecast to experience at least one day of unusually high temperatures made at least three times more likely by human-caused climate change, the analysis found.
The analysis cited the warning by the South African Weather Service (SAWS) this week that a heatwave, with persistently high temperatures, was expected in North West, most of the Free State, southern Gauteng and the north-eastern parts of the Northern Cape until Friday.
The SAWS said extremely high fire danger conditions were also expected across the Northern Cape, the eastern parts of North West and Free State, the north-eastern parts of the Western Cape, parts of Limpopo’s south-western Bushveld and several Eastern Cape municipalities, including Dr Beyers Naudé, Inxuba Yethemba and Walter Sisulu.
Temperatures of 36°C to 40°C were forecast in parts of the Northern Cape’s Namakwa district and the Western Cape interior, between 6°C and 10°C above normal for this time of year.
South Africa’s hot November conditions were also unfolding during the seasonal transition from spring to summer, when temperatures rose ahead of the arrival of sufficient atmospheric moisture to support the summer rainfall season.
“In spring we have high temperatures and not adequate moisture. So, the moisture is still going to come,” said Thokelo Chiloane, a senior forecaster at the SAWS.
Chiloane said high temperatures were characteristic of spring, when there was often a lag between rising temperatures and the increase in moisture needed for widespread rainfall.
During summer, the combination of high temperatures and greater atmospheric moisture helped drive afternoon thunderstorms, bringing rainfall and some relief from the heat.
The heat comes against the backdrop of a very strong El Niño, which is expected to influence global weather patterns and South Africa’s summer rainfall.
In its latest State of the Climate Update, released on Monday, the World Meteorological Organisation said the event was expected to be the strongest on record by December, adding to heat and extreme weather risks well into 2027.
The El Niño was also expected to affect summer rainfall, Chiloane said, contributing to drier-than-normal conditions across parts of the country.
She cautioned against attributing the current hot conditions to climate change alone, saying seasonal weather patterns and El Niño were also contributing factors.

Residents across the West Rand have been urged to prepare for a second heatwave expected to last until Friday, November 13.
Weather lover and meteorological hobbyist Juandré Vorster, known as ‘The Weather Hooligan’, warned that severe heat will grip the region over the coming days.
Vorster explained that temperatures could climb towards 40°C in parts of Pretoria and adjacent areas.
Thunderstorms expected
Vorster noted that the intense daytime heat may trigger thunderstorms across the province.
“We could see the first storm activity developing as early as Friday night, but Saturday and Sunday are looking particularly interesting for thunderstorm development across Gauteng. I’m expecting the potential for spectacular lightning displays, heavy localised downpours, strong gusty winds and possibly some isolated hail,” said Vorster.
Mogale City issues warning and urges precautionary measures
Mogale issued a warning today, November 11, on its Facebook page for residents about the upcoming second heatwave of the season.
The municipality’s assistant manager for media and public relations, Refilwe Mahlangu, said the South African Weather Service announced that temperatures are expected to reach highs of 36°C across several parts of Gauteng, including Mogale City.
Mahlangu urged residents to take precautions during the heatwave by staying hydrated, drinking plenty of water and avoiding prolonged exposure to direct sunlight.
Municipal water pressure
Mahlangu stated that the heatwave is expected to increase water consumption, which will place additional pressure on the municipal water system.
“Residents are urged to use water sparingly and avoid non-essential use, like watering gardens during the day and filling swimming pools, to help maintain sufficient supply across affected communities.”
The local municipality has appealed to residents to stay cool, keep hydrated and conserve water during the high-temperature period.
